Repairing an over-done alarplasty

An alarplasty cuts skin from the nostrils to make them smaller. That skin doesn't grow back. This guide explains, in plain words, the main repair options, what each one can and can't do, and what the research says.

Based on published studies, surgeons' public case photos and experiences patients have shared. Not medical advice.

Not sure where to start? Take the 3-question quiz →

Why this guide exists

Most of a rhinoplasty can be revised. Cartilage and bone can usually be rebuilt with grafts. An alarplasty is different: it cuts away skin, and skin doesn't grow back. That makes it one of the few steps in a nose job that can't truly be undone.

Yet many patients report waking up with an alarplasty they never agreed to. Surgery without consent is a serious violation of bodily autonomy, and patients describe lasting psychological harm, including not recognizing their own face.

This guide was put together by patients who went through it. They dug through the studies, compared hundreds of before and after photos and questioned surgeons, so the next person in the same situation doesn't have to start from zero.

Before you start

What did the alarplasty take?

The right repair depends on what's missing. Two different cuts cause two different problems.

What's actually wrong?

"My nostrils look smaller" can mean four different problems. Most people have more than one, and each points to a different repair.

The shape is wrong

A notch, a teardrop or a flat, pinched wing. You may still have enough skin, but it sits in the wrong shape.

2a. Alar lobule flap

The support is gone

The wing caves in, or the rim is pulled up, because cartilage was trimmed or a scar is pulling. Cartilage can bring back the curve without adding skin.

3. Support and lining fixes

Skin is actually missing

The opening is smaller and the flare is gone because skin was cut away. This is the hardest problem: something has to add skin or move it in.

1. Composite grafts · 2b. Island flaps

The tip angle makes it look worse

A tip turned up shows more of the inside of the nostrils, so notches stand out. Changing the angle can hide them, but it can't put skin back.

4. Derotation

Two ways to bring in skin

The trade-off with flaps: you need spare skin nearby, you make a new cut where it comes from, and small flaps can shrink unless cartilage holds them in shape.

More on this Reports, an example

Find out what was actually done

Operative reports sometimes leave out or understate the alarplasty. In one case, revision surgeons measured about 5 mm taken from each side, where the original surgeon claimed 2 mm. Get an independent surgeon to examine you and write down the measurements first.

Not every alarplasty is aggressive

1

Composite grafts

Most studiedAdds real skinSkin + cartilage from the ear

Take a small piece of your ear that has two layers, skin and the cartilage under it, and stitch it into the nose to replace what was cut.

Composite graft vs. cartilage graft

"Ear graft" can mean two different things. A cartilage graft is cartilage only: it can prop up or reshape a wing, but it adds no skin, so it can't undo an alarplasty on its own. A composite graft is skin plus cartilage (sometimes skin and fat). It's the only kind of graft that puts skin back. This section is about composite grafts.

A graft is like a cut flower in a vase. It has no roots, so it has to grow new blood vessels in its new spot. Small ones usually make it. Big ones sometimes don't.

47 of 47small grafts took. 56 patients, many after too much alar base was cut, followed for 4 years 8 months on average (Manafi 2013).
93.7%of 367 grafts in rhinoplasty patients took fully (Toriumi 2023).
87%of 15 patients were satisfied, and no graft died. Grafts were placed from inside the nostril (Front Med 2026).

Most composite graft studies are about injuries, burns and cancer, not cosmetic alarplasty. Manafi's is one of the few that includes over-cut alar bases.

1a. Internal1b. External
Where it goesInside the nostril. The wing is freed and the graft is tucked into the lining.On the outside of the wing, filling the wedge or sill that was cut.
What it can doModest extra size and a little flare.The most direct way to rebuild the shape that was cut.
Scar you'd seeOnly if someone looks up your nose.On the outside, around the patch.
Main riskShrinking back over time.Color mismatch, shrinking, not taking.
How provenSome studies for small rim defects. Not formally studied for winning back flare.Decades of studies, mostly after injury or cancer.
Can it be undone?Easier to remove.Hard. Removing it means more scars.

Surviving isn't the whole story

Most grafts take, especially small ones. But for a cosmetic repair the graft also has to look like your own skin. Shrinking, color, texture and the scar line matter even when the graft is alive. In the 2026 study, color mismatch and mild shrinking showed at 3 to 6 months, and two patients had mild pull-back later.

1a

Internal composite grafts

The middle ground

The wing is released from the inside, scar tissue is freed, and the composite graft is slipped into the nostril lining so the wing can sit further out. It doesn't rebuild the outside of the wedge, but it adds some size and flare without an outside scar. Many patients see it as the best balance.

Surgeons reported as doing it internally: Dr. Oguzhan Oguz, Dr. Shahriar Nazari (Iran), Dr. Blas García (Spain), Dr. Ahmet Halit Aydın, and reportedly Dr. Khosh (US). Dr. Göde says he now only does them internally.

1b

External composite grafts

Works, but shows

The composite graft is sewn into the outside of the wing, right where the wedge or sill was cut. It's the most direct way to rebuild the original shape, and it has decades of studies behind it. The catch is the outside scar, and ear skin doesn't always match nose skin, especially on darker skin.

Surgeons reported as doing it externally: Dr. Jason Roostaeian (US), Dr. Amir Sazgar (Iran), Dr. Shingyochi (Japan), Dr. Erkan Soylu, Dr. Fatullayev, Dr. Kidakorn Kiranantawat (Thailand, for a nostril scarred nearly shut), and Dr. Ali Manafi (in his published study).

Key examples

More external examples 1 more

Skin tone matters

Ear skin can heal lighter or darker than the skin around it, and scars hold less pigment. On darker skin that's easier to see. Patients have reported external composites healing badly on Black and East Asian skin, and Dr. Toriumi reportedly told a Black patient: "if you were Caucasian, I would consider, but as a black person, I wouldn't recommend it." The studies are mixed, and there's almost no data for the darkest skin types. If you have darker skin, ask to see healed results on people with your skin tone, and lean towards internal.

Bottom line. The most studied way to put skin back. If you want more size and can live with modest gains, an internal graft is the middle ground. External grafts rebuild the most, but the patch can show. Either way, grafts can shrink back over time.

More detail What surgeons said, research, figures, sources

What surgeons told patients

  • Dr. Oguzhan Oguz (Istanbul, August 2026) told a patient he'd only do internal grafts, never external, and advised against external flaps too. Another patient said he suggested external for her, so ask directly.
  • Dr. Sercan Göde said he used to do many composite grafts but now prefers flaps, because grafts must grow a new blood supply and can shrink.
  • Dr. Erkan Soylu turned down one patient because he only does it when the nostrils are very small. Another patient reportedly widened successfully with him.
  • Dr. Ziad Katrib uses internal grafts for pulled-up rims but turned down alarplasty repair.

What the research says

Composite grafts have more studies than anything else here, though most are about injuries, burns and cancer rather than cosmetic alarplasty.

Manafi et al., 2013 (Iran)
  • 56 patients, mostly after too much alar base was cut
  • Small grafts (skin and fat): 47 of 47 took
  • Bigger grafts with cartilage: 5 of 9 excellent, 3 acceptable, 1 failed
  • Average follow-up 4 years 8 months
  • Not advised over 2 cm. Use flaps instead
Toriumi et al., 2023 (US)
  • 367 grafts in 234 rhinoplasties
  • 93.7% took fully, 6.3% partly or fully failed
Sazgar et al., 2025 (Iran)
  • 45 people with over-cut nostril floor and wing junctions
  • No graft failures, even after past skin death
  • Breathing and appearance scores improved a lot
Asian patients, 2026
  • 15 patients, grafts placed from inside the nostril
  • No graft died; mild shrinking and color mismatch at 3 to 6 months
  • Scars "almost indistinguishable" at 1 year; 2 had mild pull-back later; 87% satisfied
Ahuja et al., 2014 (India)
  • 19 patients, all survived, all shrank a little
  • Pigment varied, like a skin graft
  • Keep grafts under 1 cm wide
Agrawal et al., 2025 (India)
  • 11 patients, skin types III to V
  • Over 90% survival, one shrank by about half

A fresh composite graft can look pale, then bluish around day 7, before it pinks up as blood vessels grow in (Jackson and Reisler, 2018). Ask your surgeon what to watch for.

2

Flaps

Skin that keeps its own blood supply

Move nearby skin into the nostril without ever cutting it off from its blood supply. Two very different sizes of flap:

2a

Alar lobule flap + ear cartilage

Best direct evidenceFixes shape, not size

If there's a little spare skin on the outside of the nostril wing, the surgeon slides it into the notch while it stays attached, and puts a curved piece of ear cartilage underneath to hold a rounder shape.

Like rearranging furniture instead of building a new room. Nothing new comes in, so the nostril doesn't get bigger, but everything sits in a nicer shape.

How it's done

The results

16patients, all treated for damage after a cosmetic nostril reduction
Every flapsurvived. One cartilage graft got infected and was removed.
2 to 3.5 mmof spare wing skin was the most a flap used

Ohba et al., 2024. The only study we found on exactly this problem: damage after cosmetic nostril reduction.

Can help if

  • You have notches, teardrop shapes or flat wings
  • There's a little spare skin on the outer wing
  • You want a natural curve more than a bigger opening

Won't help if

  • A lot of sill skin was cut
  • You mainly want bigger nostrils
  • There's no spare wing skin to move

Trade-offs

  • A small new scar, kept in the crease
  • Ear cartilage means a second small cut at the ear
  • A nostril retainer, worn for about 6 months

Not the same as making the nostril bigger

This flap moves skin you already have. It fills notches and brings back a natural curve. It doesn't replace a lot of skin that was cut away. In the study, any widening came from releasing a ligament and using cartilage to push the wings out, not from the flap itself.

Where: Dr. Norihiro Ohba, Primo Azabujuban Clinic, Tokyo. Dr. Göde and Dr. Tolga Bilece have also offered it to patients.

Ohba 2024, full paper ↗Video: the flap ↗Video: the cartilage graft ↗

More detail The study, more figures, practical notes
The study (Ohba et al., 2024)
  • 16 patients, 2016 to 2022, all after cosmetic nostril reduction
  • Main tool: curved ear cartilage, chosen to avoid the color problems of composite grafts
  • Flap added only when there was spare outer wing skin, 2 to 3.5 mm wide at most
Results
  • Every flap survived
  • Nostril shape improved in every case
  • 1 cartilage graft got infected and was removed
  • Typical follow-up about 9 months; retainer worn 6 months
Good to know
  • To widen, the authors release a ligament and use cartilage to push the wings outward
  • Small study, run by the clinic's own surgeons
  • It needs cartilage support, or the groove can flatten

For tight scars and tethering next to the wings, patients have also recommended the Japanese surgeon @tetuichiro, though he wasn't taking overseas patients when asked.

Source

  • Ohba N, Haraoka G, Ohba M, Takahashi N. Treatment of Alar Deformity After Cosmetic Surgery. Plast Reconstr Surg Glob Open 2024;12(11):e6327. Full text
2b

Lip or cheek island flap

Promising, unprovenThe only option that adds living skin

A small island of skin from the upper lip or cheek is moved into the nostril while it stays attached to a stem of blood vessels, so the wing can be pushed back out.

Like moving a garden hose to another plant without ever unplugging it from the tap.

Dr. Sercan Göde (Izmir) is the surgeon best known for it. It works well for rebuilding columellas, and he started using it for alarplasty reversal in 2026.

0published studies of this flap for repairing a cosmetic alarplasty
103cancer patients had a similar nose island flap, and no flap was lost (Tregaskiss 2014). The flap type is reliable; its use here is new.
5patients: a flap from the crease moved a pulled-in nostril base outward (Patel 2022)

Why it's promising

  • The only option that brings new living skin, so in theory the most size
  • Can't die like a graft
  • Nearby skin usually matches better than ear skin

Reasons for caution

  • Very new for alarplasty. Most photos are from the operating table
  • One patient who spoke to 20+ lip flap patients says their bases narrowed again within weeks
  • Skin-only flaps can shrink and flatten the sills
  • Some patients got clear scars on the sill or lip

Established surgery, new use

Moving skin on its own blood supply is standard in cancer reconstruction. Using it to reverse a cosmetic alarplasty isn't, yet: no long-term series shows how the scars, the shrinking and the extra width hold up.

More detail How it works, what surgeons said, research, 7 more examples

How it was explained to a patient

The surgeon cuts along the crease, keeps that skin attached, and turns it in to make a new sill, which lets the wing move outward. Cartilage or an internal graft goes underneath for support. Dr. Göde told a patient he'd turn a lip flap toward the wing rim to add width. He also said he hadn't done it on a Black patient yet.

What other surgeons said

  • Dr. Oguz: he's done cheek (nasolabial) flaps for cancer patients and the scars look bad; flaps are too much just for flare.
  • A US surgeon: does flap reconstruction often for cancer patients but would never recommend it for cosmetic patients; his note called flap rotations for alarplasty "very risky."

What doctors have published

No study has tested lip island flaps for cosmetic alarplasty reversal yet, but the building blocks exist:

  • Tregaskiss et al., 2014: 103 patients had a wing rebuilt with an island flap from the side of the nose, after skin cancer. No flap was lost, and three surgeons rated most results good to excellent.
  • Patel et al., 2022: a flap from the crease moved a pulled-in nostril base outward in 5 patients, with a rim graft for support.
  • Nadjmi et al., 2022: rebuilt a damaged wing with a flap from the opposite nostril base, with matching color.
  • Selçuk et al., 2012: cheek flaps with cartilage support for wing defects. Manafi points to flaps like these for defects over 2 cm.
  • Le Diep Linh et al., 2024: upper lip island flaps to rebuild columellas.

More examples

Sources

  2. Patel N, et al. Inferiorly Based Alar Groove Flap for Correction of Alar Base Malposition and Nasal Stenosis. Plast Reconstr Surg Glob Open 2022;10:e4334. Full text

Bottom line. For notches and teardrop shapes with spare wing skin, the alar lobule flap with cartilage is the best-studied fix, but it won't make nostrils much bigger. Lip and cheek island flaps are the only real hope for a lot of new skin, but there are almost no healed, long-term results yet. Many patients try gentler fixes first and wait for more results.

3

Support and lining fixes

Fixes support, not skinOften done first, or alongside

Rebuild the frame under the skin: cartilage to hold the wing's curve, and extra lining inside the nostril when the rim has been pulled up.

Like fixing a sagging tent by replacing the poles, not the fabric.

3.4 to 1.5 mmaverage rim pull-up before and after rim grafts plus V-Y advancement, in 25 patients (Zhan and Wang 2026)
2.7 mmaverage improvement in pulled-up rims with cartilage extension grafts, in 47 patients. Scarring limited 7 of them (Marianetti 2020).
Noneof these add outside skin. They fix collapse and pulled-up rims.
  • Cartilage grafts. Pulled-up or collapsed wings can often be fixed with cartilage before touching skin.
  • V-Y advancement. A small V-shaped flap of lining inside the nostril is slid forward and stitched as a Y, adding lining so the rim can come down. Paired with rim grafts, it worked well for pulled-up rims in a 2026 study. It adds inside lining, not outside skin, and few surgeons offer it for alarplasty damage. At least one botched case with outside scars has been reported.
  • Scar release. Loosening tight scars, sometimes with a Z-shaped cut, can help with smiling, tightness and itching. It won't make nostrils wider.
  • Scar care. Laser, dermabrasion, tretinoin and medical tattooing all helped some patients and not others. Dermabrasion carries pigment risk on darker skin.
  • Wait for swelling to settle. Early on, nostrils can look smaller and stiffer than they'll end up.

Bottom line. Often the first step, and often done alongside the other repairs. It fixes collapse and pulled-up rims. It doesn't replace skin that was cut away.

Zhan and Wang 2026, V-Y ↗Marianetti 2020 ↗

Research to watch

Verteporfin, a drug being studied for healing with less scarring (Dr. Michael Longaker's lab, Stanford), and lab-grown tissue that survives until it connects to blood vessels (EU research project). Neither is available as a treatment yet.

4

Derotation

Helper onlyOnly if your tip was turned upAdds no tissue

Tip the point of the nose down a little, so less of the inside of the nostrils shows.

Think of a mug. Tilt it up and you see right inside. Tilt it down and you don't. Derotation tilts the nose down so the uneven nostrils hide.

Why it's last: no study has tested derotation as an alarplasty repair, and it can't put back skin that was cut. It can make what you have look its best, usually alongside one of the repairs above.

Can help if

  • Your tip got turned up in surgery
  • Your alarplasty was mild to moderate
  • Your nostrils look better when you push the tip down

Won't help if

  • A lot of skin was cut
  • Your tip wasn't turned up
  • Your wing was stitched too low compared to the columella

Trade-offs

  • Usually needs a strong support graft (an SEG, often rib), which can feel stiff
  • Overdone, it can look older or droopy
  • It's another full nose surgery

Key examples

Bottom line. Only worth it if your tip was turned up. It makes what you have left look its best, often in the same surgery as other repairs. It won't bring back what was cut.

More detail Why it might work, patient experiences, sources

Why it might help

Alarplasty damage is easiest to see when a lot of the nostril shows. Many patients also have their tips turned up in the same surgery, which puts the notches and uneven sides on display. Surgeons do treat nostril show as a real, fixable problem and even classify how the rims sit (Rohrich and Afrooz, 2019). But nobody has published derotation as an alarplasty repair. The idea comes from patients comparing hundreds of before and after photos.

The mirror test

In a mirror, gently push your nose tip down using your upper lip and cheek muscles. If the wings flare out more, rotation is probably part of your problem. If nothing changes, you're most likely missing skin. It's a rough clue, not a diagnosis.

What patients report

  • If there is more rotation, there is more nostril show. So you see the alarplasty deformity more easily.A patient who researched derotation
  • Nostril flare can be currently improved with downrotation. Flaps and skin grafts do not help for flare.A patient with eight surgeries, who was against derotation at first
  • With severe alar issues, simple derotation will not fix the issue.The same patient, months earlier, about her own case. Derotation pulled her nostrils further up, not out.

One patient's nostrils looked wider after his revision even though their size didn't change: his surgeon made the tip stick out less and propped up the collapsed wings. Later, a surgeon told the same patient his real issue was how the rim had been stitched, not rotation, and a US surgeon turned him down, saying his skin might not allow the derotation he wanted. Get examined before betting on this.

US surgeons named most often for strong derotation: Dr. Sam Most and Dr. Ari Hyman. Dr. Scott Owen and Dr. Steitz also came up.

Putting it together

One table to remember

Moving skin, adding skin and adding support are three different jobs. Most repairs do only one or two of them, which is why they're often combined.

MethodMoves skin?Adds skin?Adds support?Best forMain limit

1b. External composite graftNoYesUsuallyRebuilding a cut wedge or sillVisible patch, color, shrinking
2a. Alar lobule flapYes, nearby skinNo new skinYes, with ear cartilageNotches, teardrops, flat wingsNeeds spare wing skin; only a few mm
2b. Lip or cheek island flapYes, with its blood supplyYes, brings it inMay need cartilageA lot of missing skinLong-term scars and width unknown
3. Cartilage graftNoNoYesCollapsed or flat wingsCan't replace missing skin
3. V-Y advancementYes, inside liningInside lining onlyOften with a rim graftPulled-up rimsDoesn't add outside skin

Before you book

Questions to ask any surgeon

These move the talk away from vague words like "reversal" and towards exactly what will be done.

  1. What exactly is missing?

    Outside skin, inside lining, cartilage support? Or is the tissue there but scarred into the wrong shape? Is my tip turned up? Each has a different fix.

  2. Draw every cut on my photo

    On a photo of my nose from below: where does new tissue come from, where does it go, and where will every scar be? Inside or outside?

  3. What keeps it alive?

    For a graft: how big is it, and what will feed it? For a flap: where is its blood supply?

  4. What keeps it from shrinking back?

    Cartilage support, scar release, a retainer? What have you seen after 12 months? Grafts and flaps have been reported to shrink back within weeks.

  5. Show me the same operation, healed

    From below and from the front, 6 to 12 months or more later, on skin like mine and a problem like mine. Not on the operating table. Can I talk to them?

  6. What if we do less?

    A smaller fix for the shape may be safer than chasing every lost millimeter.

  7. How many millimeters, exactly?

    How much will you add or remove, and will it be written in my report?

  8. Stitches and scar care

    Which stitches will you use outside, and when do they come out? Facial stitches usually come out around day 7. What's the plan for scars afterwards?

  9. Can it be undone, and is it all in writing?

    If I don't like it, what then? Will you do anything I haven't agreed to in writing? Some patients have woken up with an alarplasty they never asked for.

    "Larger and better nostrils are possible." Rib cartilage plus composite grafts, on darker skin.

  • Dr. Sercan Göde, 2024 Internal

    An alar retraction repair. One patient recalls this case differently, as outside grafts that scarred, so ask him directly.

1b. External composite grafts

  • Dr. Jason Roostaeian (US) External

    "Correcting the over-resected alar base." These appear to have healed well, with visibly bigger nostrils.

  • Dr. Amir Sazgar (Tehran), October 2026 External

    One month after rebuilding a nose with six failed surgeries and past skin death. Too early to judge the scars.

  • Dr. Kidakorn Kiranantawat (Thailand), 2024 External

    A nostril scarred nearly shut after cosmetic surgery. The scar was released, then a skin-and-cartilage graft from the ear was placed on the raw edge of the opened nostril. Shown 1 year and 10 months later.

  • Dr. Shingyochi (Japan), February 2026 External (A 2025 case)

    A difficult alar revision. You can see the old alarplasty scars at the base of the nostrils.

2b. Lip and cheek island flaps

  • Dr. Sercan Göde

    "Alar base reduction reversal." A lip island flap case, before and after.

  • Dr. Sercan Göde, September 2026

    "Alar base reversing by local island flaps." Taken on the operating table, so expect it to settle.

  • Dr. Sercan Göde, March 2026

    A complicated revision with flaps. The video has close-ups of the scars, and opinions differ on how visible they are.

  • Dr. Sercan Göde, April 2026

    Five months after a complex revision. Patients who reviewed it found the scars noticeable even with a filter.

  • Dr. Sercan Göde, January 2026

    Tip and columella skin death, two months after reconstruction. Shared to show how his flaps work.

  • Dr. Sercan Göde

    A revision that lengthened the columella and improved retraction. An island flap appears to have been used.

  • Dr. Sercan Göde, March 2025

    An alar retraction repair. Some patients noticed teardrop notches afterwards.

  • Dr. Oguzhan Oguz, June 2026

    "When tissue is lost, reconstruction becomes the only option." Patients have felt his flaps were less refined than Göde's.

  • Dr. Sercan Göde, March 2026

    An extreme revision on a Black patient after skin death. A very severe case, and the scars are visible.

3. Support and lining fixes

  • Dr. Ziad Katrib

    Reinforcing a weak tip with rib cartilage. Structure before skin.

  • Dr. Shingyochi (Japan), March 2026

    Fixing the scar and the shape around the nostril.

4. Derotation

  • Dr. Sam Most, June 2023

    A long-term revision result. The nostrils look fuller after derotation. This patient never had an alarplasty. Video, so play it on Instagram.

  • Dr. Ari Hyman, August 2025

    Seven months after a revision to bring down an upturned tip.

  • Dr. Ari Hyman, August 2023

    Three months after a revision to correct uneven nostrils. Shared as an example of strong derotation.

Word list What the doctor words mean
Ala (alae)
The nostril wing.
Alar lobule
The soft, rounded part of the wing near the bottom.
Alar crease
The groove where the wing meets your cheek.
Sill
The little floor at the bottom of each nostril.
Columella
The strip of skin between the nostrils.
Alarplasty
Surgery that cuts skin from the nostrils to make them smaller. Also called alar base reduction.
Weir excision
An alarplasty that cuts both the sill and a wedge from the wing.
Flare
How much the wings curve outward.
Notching, teardrop deformity
A dent in the nostril edge, or a nostril pulled into a teardrop shape.
Retraction
When the nostril rim is pulled up too high.
Nostril show
How much of the nostril openings you can see.
Rotation, derotation
Turning the nose tip up, or back down.
SEG
Septal extension graft. A strong cartilage piece that sets where the tip points.
Cartilage graft
Cartilage only. Adds support and shape, not skin.
Composite graft
Skin plus cartilage (or fat), moved as one piece. Adds skin.
Flap
Tissue moved while staying attached to its blood supply.
Island flap
A flap attached only by a small stem of blood vessels, so it can move further.
Table photo
A photo taken on the operating table. Results look better than they'll end up.
Fitzpatrick type
A scale from I (very fair) to VI (deeply pigmented). Matters for scars and pigment.

This is not medical advice. It summarizes published studies, surgeons' public posts and experiences patients have shared. Every nose is different. Get examined by qualified surgeons before deciding anything.

Patient experiences are paraphrased or quoted without names. Surgeon comments are as reported by patients after their own consultations. Study figures are shown unchanged from open-access papers with credit and license. Instagram images are credited and link to the original posts.
